messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

Given your two original images of the femur "61 Ks" and "2 Ks", it seems you are expecting these two to look about the same.

However, the original individual data will not look the same after GPA. This is because you included semilandmarks in your analysis, these will slide to a certain degree depending on the variation of all of your other individual samples, to minimize some criterion like Procrustes distance or bending energy. You seemed to have used the default option for the ProcD= argument in gpagen meaning you are currently sliding semilandmarks to minimize bending energy.

You might also be wondering why 61 Ks looks like an impossible femur shape (assuming the landmarks and semilandmarks were placed on the outline of the femur, judging by your original data). This is may be due to the semilandmarks but could be influenced by many aspects of data collection and analysis. Rather than potentially misleading you on this front, I will defer to more experienced folks who can provide better feedback.

Best,
Bryan

messages.body_plain:
There must be some issue with how you grabbing them when creating the second dataset in a different order.  If the objects are grabbed correctly and placed in a new dataframe before GPA, all will be the same.

Here is a repeatable example showing what I mean:

library(geomorph)

data(plethodon)

data1 <- plethodon$land[,,c(1,2)]

data2 <- plethodon$land[,,c(2,1)]  #opposite order

out1 <- gpagen(data1, PrinAxes = FALSE)

out2 <- gpagen(data2, PrinAxes = FALSE)

plot(data1[,,1], asp=1)

plot(out1$coords[,,1], asp=1)

plot(out2$coords[,,2], asp=1)

Note that the plots of the specimen do not change when the order is reversed.

I suggest you go back to how you created the two datasets of different order to look for an error in coding at that pre-processing step.

Shadia,

There are many ways to calculate the matrix of Procrustes distances. The code I provided you earlier accomplished it using arguments within geomorph.

If you want a step-by-step approach, here is one:

library(geomorph)

data(plethodon)

Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land)

shape <- two.d.array(Y.gpa$coords)

Pdistances <- dist(shape) # a lower-triangular matrix of pairwise Procrustes distances

Dean

messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

we are still accepting applications of interest for participating in the course in Geometric Morphometrics using R <https://geomorphr.github.io/GMcourse/> by the geomorph R-package development team, to be held in Barcelona (Spain), on May 8-12, 2023.

The deadline for applications is November 30, 2022.

The goal of the workshop is to provide participants with both working knowledge of the theory of geometric morphometrics, as well as practical training in the application of these methods.

The course will occur in the Faculty of Biology of the University of Barcelona <https://www.ub.edu/portal/web/biologia/> and is organized by the Department of Evolutionary Biology, Ecology and Environmental Science <https://www.ub.edu/portal/web/dp-beeca/> and the Institute of Research in Biodiversity <http://www.ub.edu/irbio/home>.

This is considered a post-graduate course, approved by the Faculty of Biology of the UB, and it corresponds to 3 ECTS units, for students interested in validating and transferring credits for it. It is, however, open as an international workshop to participants at any stage of their academic career.

The cost of the course will be of 350 euros per participant.

To apply for participating in the course please feel in the application form here <https://forms.gle/SppEEYe6cYXmdp9q7>

Up to 25 participants will be accepted on the basis of their academic career stage (priority given to PhD students and early-career researchers) and relevance of the course for their research.

Admitted participants will be informed until December 15, 2022.

On behalf of the geomorph team and the local organizing committee

Antigoni

--

Antigoni Kaliontzopoulou

Hello,

I have run into an issue warping 3D meshes to targets (in this case to PC extremes) using the plotRefToTarget function. I can get the surface to warp, but the warp does not match the PC extreme I have designated. Effectively, the surface file is smooshed anterolaterally which is not accurate to the variation captured in the PC. I have been able to plot a wireframe of the PC extremes using the plotRefToTarget function successfully, but I am unable to warp the surface.

I think the error is coming in at the creation of the average mesh, specifically at  'mean.coords' (below) as I am using the procrustes transformed coordinates which technically would not align with the .ply file. However, when I try to load in my coordinates from the .landmarkASCII file (i.e. #mean.coords2) I get the following error: "Error in warpRefMesh(mean.ply, mean.coords2, avg, color = NULL, centered = FALSE) :  Input must be a p-x-k matrix of landmark coordinates". I'm not sure how to correct this issue.

Does anyone have any advice on resolving this?

I have provided a my code here:

lmcoords <- coords.all[["coords"]]    # coordinates created from multiple files for the same species using 'combine.subsets'
Y.gpa <- gpagen(lmcoords, Proj = TRUE, PrinAxes = TRUE)
ref <-mshape(Y.gpa$coords)

PCA <- gm.prcomp(Y.gpa$coords)
PC1min <- PCA$shapes$shapes.comp1$min

plotRefToTarget(M1 = mean.coords, M2 = PC1min, mesh = averagemesh, color = gray, method = "surface")

Hi Maddy,

I encountred the same problem in the past and I found some code to solve this likely on this forum. Anyway here it is:

#Find specimen closer to mean, useful to create warp mesh

##Create warp mesh, to use as reference for visualization of analyses
ref_mesh <- warpRefMesh(mesh = mesh_3D, mesh.coord = warp_specimen, ref = mean_shape, color = "gray", centered = FALSE)

Then ref_mesh is what you need to apply plotRefToTarget to to get your PC extremes.
To scale the mesh I use the free software Meshlab. I usally need to reduce the mesh to about 100th of its original size (if it was 20 cm in lenght, it will become 0.02 cm), but that will depend on your samples. Just look at the differences in decimals you get from the range function. If the mesh shows values like 20 - 30 and your warp speciemen coordinates are 0.02 - 0.03 you would need to reduce the mesh by 100 and so forth.
Depending on how great the deformation is and your specific samples, the plotRefToTarget mesh might be better or worse than just using points for example, but if it works well it's a very nice visualization.

Hope this helps!
Best wishes,
Agnese

Hello,

Thank you both for your replies! I was able to properly warp the mesh.

The issue was in the coordinates I was using to create the average mesh (as Murat pointed out). In my original code I was calling the gpa transformed coordinates of the mean species which did not fit the scale of .ply file. I had suspected this was the issue, but I was having trouble loading in the untransformed coordinates without an error message. I am also combining several landmark sets per species (1 traditional landmark file and 2 sliding landmark files) using the 'combine.subsets' function to create my 'coords.all' assignment. As I learned through troubleshooting this, while you can specify the combine.subsets function not to perform a GPA it will still adjust all centroid sizes to 1.0 (unless otherwise specified) which would have also made it inappropriate to use to create the average mesh. Knowing this, I decided to combine all three landmarks files for each species by hand and was able to call the untransformed coords for the mean species to create the average mesh.

I'm not sure if it's helpful, but I am including the code I used to do this with annotation:

## WARPING SURFACES ##
    GDF <- geomorph.data.frame(landmarks = coords.all)    # could probably use your matrix of lm coords, but as I was having issues getting my coords from my matrix (coords.all) so I created a geomorph dataframe with raw coords

    Y.gpa <- gpagen(coords.all, curves = sliders)    # run gpa with curves designated (for my data the slider were defined using 'define.sliders' function)
    ref <-mshape(Y.gpa$coords)                               # get coords for the mean shape from the transformed landmark matrix

    var <- Y.gpa[["coords"]]
    avg <-mshape(var)     # calculate the mean shape
    findMeanSpec(var)    # identify species closest to mean

    mean.ply <- read.ply("Tamiasciurus-hudsonicus.ply", ShowSpecimen=FALSE)    # load the .ply for the mean species
    mean.coords <- coords.all[,,38]            # get the untransformed coordinates for the mean specimen/species (38 is the sequence number for the mean species (i.e. Tamiasciurus hudsonicus))
    ygpa.mc <http://ygpa.mc> <- Y.gpa$coords[,,38]             # get transformed coords (from Y.gpa) for the mean specimen/species

    averagemesh <- warpRefMesh(mean.ply, mean.coords, avg, color=NULL, centered=FALSE)   # create a mesh of the average shape

    PCA <- gm.prcomp(Y.gpa$coords)                       # need to run a PCA to get the extremes for PCs
    PC1min <- PCA$shapes$shapes.comp1$min    # identify the coords for the min of PC1 (comp1)

    plotRefToTarget(M1 = ygpa.mc <http://ygpa.mc>, M2 = PC1min, mesh = averagemesh, method = "surface")    # warp averagemesh to the coords at PC1min

Best,
Maddy

messages.body_plain:
Dear Werner,

thank you for your help. Getting a scree plot is useful, but your example uses gm.prcomp, which produces different PCs than the model itself.

By looking at the code for the plot.lm.rrpp function, I found out how it's done and now use the same method:

f <- as.matrix(rrpp.1$LM$fitted)
pca <- prcomp(f)

var_explained = pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)

library(ggplot2)

a <- qplot(c(1:26), var_explained) +

  geom_line() +
  xlab("Principal Component") +
  ylab("Variance Explained") +

  ylim(0, 1)+theme_classic()+
 geom_hline(yintercept=0.02, linetype="dotted") # to highlight the 2% explained variation threshold

require(vegan)
summary(pca) #an alternative to var_explained
eigenvals(pca) # to extract eigenvalues

Thanks again,
Bob
